verdict: Avoid new dye/intermediate exposure in Kota until local demand and safety records are proven; lend only to spillover suppliers of large solvent-grade peers with clean fire-safety audits.
title: Kota Chemicals, Dyes & Intermediates: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Kota's chemical units are small-batch converters: they buy solvents, dye intermediates and inorganic inputs, run reaction and drying lines, and sell to textile processors, dye makers and formulators.** Cash is made on conversion margin, not on the molecule; value sits in the reactor, the boiler and the effluent consent, and cash sits in inventory and receivables. **The cycle is short on the sales side but long on the input side** — most units hold feedstock against price moves, so working capital is the real exposure, not the plant. Capex is modest but continuous: reactors, scrubbers, ETP upgrades. **So when a proposal lands, check the ETP consent and the fire NOC first; if either is expired or pending, ask for the renewal order before you look at the numbers.**

## What has changed now
**The local signal is weak.** Rajasthan GST collections are -4.7% Apr-to-date against India +6.1%, 10.8 pp slower [D], and electricity demand is +4.0% against India +9.5%, 5.5 pp slower [D]. **National output for NIC 20 is -0.5% YoY and -1.2% Apr-to-date [D].** On the ground, a Kota chemical factory fire from a short circuit took two hours to control [1][2][3] — dated February 2026, so treat it as a safety-record fact, not a demand fact. **Peer results are the counterpoint:** Aarti Industries reported Q2 FY27 revenue up 75% to ₹3,668 crore and net profit up 58.5% [6], with PAT at ₹169 crore on 30% volume growth [5]. **Read this as large, export-linked specialty players doing well while small local converters face a slower state economy** — the two are not the same borrower. ## Where the growth is
**Pursue suppliers and job-workers to the large specialty chains, not standalone dye units.** Aarti's volume-led quarter [4][7] means more outsourced intermediate conversion and more solvent and packaging demand in the belt. **Target units with a single large customer on a written supply agreement, a working ETP, and a fire audit in the last twelve months.** Avoid traders who hold stock against price and units with no captive effluent treatment. **If the borrower's top customer is a trader rather than a manufacturer, ask for the end-buyer name and the last three invoices.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure as cash-flow lending against a drawing-power limit, not a term loan for expansion.** Rating commentary flags elevated working-capital intensity in high-growth chemical operations [9], and capex funded from internal accrual with minimal external debt is the pattern that holds [8]. **Take stock and receivable statements every month, GST returns every month, and the electricity bill every month** — power is the cheapest production proxy in this belt. **Covenant on ETP consent validity and fire NOC renewal; if either lapses, freeze the limit.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for falling power consumption with flat sales, rising receivables days, and any repeat short-circuit or fire incident.** The February fire [1][2][3] shows how fast a small unit loses two months of output. **If the borrower's GST turnover drops two quarters running while state GST is already -4.7% [D], reduce the limit.** Sources say little about Kota specifically beyond the fire; lean on first principles and the peer read.
watch: Two consecutive quarters of falling turnover -> cut limit by half
Power units down >20% with flat sales -> site visit within 7 days
Fire NOC and ETP consent register (quarterly)
Any lapse or pending renewal -> freeze disbursement
Receivable days up >15 days -> ask for customer-wise ageing
